articles.title: Russia eyes India’s regional aviation market at first Innoprom expo in New Delhi
articles.text:
New Delhi: Russia is looking beyond the defence sector and wants to tap into India’s rapidly expanding civil aviation market, with its state-owned United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) pitching a range of Russian passenger aircraft for regional connectivity.
It is also offering localisation of production and MRO (Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul) facilities in the country.
UAC, the umbrella organisation for Russia’s major aircraft manufacturers like the Sukhoi, MiG, Ilyushin, Tupolev among others is showcasing three of its latest commercial aircraft at the first-ever ‘Innoprom.India’ exhibition in New Delhi.
The aircraft being showcased are the IL-114-300 turboprop, SJ-100 short-range jet and MC-21 medium-range airliner.
The exhibition is being held from 9 to 11 September at the Bharat Mandapam, coinciding with the BRICS Leaders’ Summit. Innoprom began in 2010 in Ekaterinburg as a business-to-business industrial exhibition and is being held in India for the first time.
The Russian pitch comes as India seeks to expand regional air connectivity.
Under the Modified UDAN Scheme approved in March, the government plans to develop 100 airports from existing unserved airstrips to enhance regional connectivity, in line with the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision of infrastructure expansion and transforming India into a globally competitive aviation ecosystem with a total outlay of Rs.12,159 crore over the next eight years.
UAC is seeking to position its aircraft across different segments of this emerging market.
The company says the IL-114-300 could be used to connect smaller cities and towns under the UDAN programme, particularly from airports with limited infrastructure. The SJ-100, a short-range narrow-body jet capable of carrying up to 103 passengers, is being positioned for routes linking major cities with regional centres and smaller towns. The larger MC-21 is intended for higher-demand domestic routes, the UAC said in a statement.
Russia has been trying to rebuild its commercial aviation industry around domestically produced aircraft with its own components after the post-2022 disruption of access to Western aerospace technology and supply chains.
As part of the Innoprom business programme, UAC is organising a session titled ‘Partnership Takes Flight: Towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat through Regional Aviation Projects’, where it plans to present its proposals for using Russian aircraft in India’s regional aviation network.
The company is also pitching localisation rather than merely aircraft sales.
SJ-100 and HAL partnership
The most significant of the Russian push is the proposed production of the SJ-100 in India through a partnership with state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).
UAC and HAL signed an agreement in January this year for cooperation on licensed production of the SJ-100 in India. Under the agreement, HAL is to receive rights to manufacture and sell the aircraft, including assemblies, parts and components required for maintenance and repair, while UAC will assist in establishing and upgrading HAL’s production facilities.
The partnership follows an MoU signed by the two companies in Moscow in October 2025.
The SJ-100 is a short-range narrow-body aircraft with a capacity of up to 103 passengers. As part of import-substitution efforts, the aircraft is equipped with Russian PD-8 engines, as well as domestic landing gear, avionics, an auxiliary power unit, and other systems. It is designed to foster regional air travel that bypasses major aviation hubs.
UAC CEO Vadim Badekha said the two sides have now made substantial progress on the licensing agreement.
“We are continuing the work initiated at the ‘Wings of India’ exhibition last January. Over the past six months, we have made significant progress in negotiations and reached a number of agreements regarding the IL-114-300, which we will sign at INNOPROM India,” Badekha said.
On the SJ-100 partnership with HAL, he said more than 80 percent of the licensing agreement had been finalised and that the two sides expected to sign it soon. “We expect to conclude a contract with the first Indian operator at the upcoming Aero India 2027 exhibition.”
The regional aviation circuit within India is gathering steam. Earlier this month, Goa-based airline FLY91 placed an order for 40 ATR 72-600 turboprops.
IL-114-300 for smaller airports
The other aircraft being pushed is the IL-114-300, a turboprop designed for regional operations.
UAC says it is designed to develop regional air connectivity. It is capable of operating autonomously from small airfields—regardless of their infrastructure—as well as from short runways, it said.
The company had already begun discussions with Indian operators following Wings India 2026 in Hyderabad. UAC had signed a preliminary agreement with Hyderabad-based Flamingo Aerospace for six IL-114-300 aircraft, aimed at operations serving underserved routes and smaller airports.
Badekha said agreements related to the IL-114-300 would be signed during Innoprom.India.
The MC-21, meanwhile, represents Russia’s attempt to enter the much larger medium-range passenger-aircraft segment. It is designed to compete in a market dominated globally by aircraft such as the Airbus A320 family and Boeing 737 family.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

articles.title: India and US sign deal for Javelin missiles, the plan eventually is co-production
articles.text:
New Delhi: India have signed a deal with the US for the acquisition of Javelin anti-tank guided missile systems for the Indian Army. This marks India’s formal entry as a customer of the famed shoulder-fired weapon even as both countries work towards its eventual joint production in India.
The US Embassy in India said Friday that the Indian Army had signed a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA) for the purchase of the Javelin. “The United States welcomes the Indian Army’s signing of a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA) for the purchase of the Javelin,” the embassy said in a statement.
The agreement, it added, “opens the door for future collaboration between the U.S. and Indian defense industries”.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said the agreement demonstrated the depth of American support for the Indian Army and created “new opportunities for our defense industries to work together”.
The signing of the LOA is significant as it moves the Javelin procurement from the stage of a US-approved possible Foreign Military Sale to an actual contracted acquisition.
The immediate requirement is being met through an emergency procurement, while India and the US are simultaneously working on a much larger proposal for joint manufacturing of the missile in India.
Also read: Emergency procurement done, India & US working on co-manufacturing Javelin anti-tank missiles
What India is buying
The US Defence Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA) had in November last year notified the US Congress of a possible Foreign Military Sale to India of the Javelin Missile System and associated equipment for an estimated $45.7 million.
India had requested 100 FGM-148 Javelin rounds, one additional Javelin missile for “fly-to-buy” evaluation and 25 Javelin Lightweight Command Launch Units (LwCLU), also referred to as Javelin Block 1 Command Launch Units.
Great news! India plans to acquire Javelin, the world’s premier anti-tank system, strengthening the U.S.-India defense cooperation. But what makes the U.S.-made Javelin so effective? Swipe to learn more… pic.twitter.com/Qt79aZDDVk
— U.S. Embassy India (@USAndIndia) August 28, 2026
The package includes training equipment, missile simulation rounds, a battery coolant unit, technical manuals, lifecycle support, spare parts and systems integration and testing.
The signing of the LOA now means that India has formally contracted for this package. Though the final numbers bought is unspecified, it is learnt that India has ordered 60 missiles and fewer launchers than originally plannedl with the deal now costing Rs 294 crore.
The Javelin is a medium-range, fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile that can be operated by a single soldier. Weighing about 15.9 kg, it is designed to engage armoured vehicles as well as fortified positions.
The weapon has acquired considerable battlefield fame through its extensive use by Ukrainian forces against Russian armour during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. It is operated by the US military and more than two dozen international customers.
Emergency buy before Indian production
The immediate procurement, however, is not the end goal for India.
Sources in the defence and security establishment said the present purchase is essentially a one-off emergency acquisition while New Delhi and Washington continue discussions on setting up a manufacturing capability for the Javelin in India.
The idea of producing the missile domestically has been under discussion for some time.
As reported by ThePrint, in July last year, India submitted a proposal to the US for co-production of Javelin missiles.
This followed an agreement assigned between State-owned Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) with the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV), owned by Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, in February last year to explore opportunities for manufacturing the weapon in India.
Lockheed Martin had then said the agreement would allow the JJV to evaluate the possibility of manufacturing Javelin in India to meet potential future requirements of the Indian Ministry of Defence and strengthen India’s anti-tank capabilities.
The larger co-production proposal is, therefore, strategically more important than the initial 100-missile purchase.
If concluded, it would give India access not merely to the weapon but potentially to a domestic manufacturing ecosystem around one of the world’s most widely used man-portable anti-armour systems.
The 17-year journey
In June 2024, ThePrint reported that the deal expanded to an Israeli system, and soon, an indigenous solution, 15 years after the initial decision. But India and the US were back at the negotiating table for the joint production of the shoulder-mounted Javelin anti-tank guided missiles.
About 15 years after the initial decision was taken only to be spiked later for an Israeli system and then for an indigenous solution, India and the US are back to the negotiating table for the joint production of the shoulder mounted Javelin anti-tank guided missiles.
It was way back in August 2010 that India publicly announced its plans to acquire the Javelins. In a written reply in the Lok Sabha, the then Defence Minister A.K. Antony informed Parliament that his ministry was planning to issue a Letter of Request to the US for procurement of 3rd Generation Anti-Tank Guided Missile (ATGM), Javelin.
He had said that the procurement was being planned under the US FMS (Foreign Military Sale) route and would involve transfer of technology.
Back then in 2010, the Army had a shortfall of 44,000 ATGMs of various kinds against a sanctioned holding strength of about 81,000. The Army till then was only operating the 2nd generation 2-km-range Milan of French origin and 4-km-range Russian Konkurs ATGMs.
However, news came in 2012 that the Javelin deal hit a roadblock over transfer of critical technology and reluctance of the American government to participate in the field trials.
Manufactured under a joint venture of Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, the missile till then had been showcased only at joint exercises held between both the countries.
India then decided to buy the Israeli Spike ATGM but the larger procurement plan failed with the DRDO saying they can make a similar system. Eventually, the Army bought limited numbers of Spike in multiple orders.
(Edited by Ajeet Tiwari)
